title: Dating app use and depression symptoms in adolescents
authors: Nagata JM, Domingue SK, Diep T, Helmer CK, Al-Shoaibi AAA, Ganson KT, Testa A, He J, Baker FC, Lavender JM

primary_models.name: Multivariable linear regression of parent-reported CBCL depression symptoms on lifetime dating app use, adjusted for sociodemographics and site
primary_models.location_in_paper: Table 2, adjusted columns (p. 3); reported in Results p. 3-4 and Abstract; interpreted in Discussion p. 4
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional analysis of a single ABCD wave (Year 5 follow-up, 2021-2023). Dating app use and depression symptoms measured at the same visit. One observation per adolescent; no repeated measures and no time interactions.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 6.0, Year 5 follow-up, adolescents aged 13-16 years. Of those enrolled, 3,305 were missing depression symptom data, 51 missing dating app data and 162 missing sociodemographic data, giving 8,444 complete cases (Appendix A). Missing data were handled with multiple imputation by chained equations (predictive mean matching, MAR assumption), imputing dating app use and depression symptoms from covariate information; final analytic N = 11,530. Mean age 15.0 years (SD 0.6, range 13.3-16.7); 47.9% female, 52.1% male; 52.7% White, 19.9% Black, 17.0% Latino/Hispanic, 6.1% Asian, 3.5% Native American, 0.9% Other (47.3% racial and ethnic minorities). Household income: 12.7% <=$24,999, 12.6% $25,000-49,999, 11.2% $50,000-74,999, 11.4% $75,000-99,999, 33.3% $100,000-199,999, 18.8% >=$200,000. Parent education: 14.7% high school or less, 85.3% college or more (Table 1, post-imputation).
primary_models.iv: Lifetime dating app use from the adolescent item "Have you ever used a dating app?" (yes, no, don't know what that is), entered as a three-level categorical variable with "never used" as reference. Distribution after imputation: never used 98.8%, used 0.9%, don't know what it is 0.3% (Table 1). No information on recency, frequency, platform, or time spent was used; current use (4 participants) and weekly time on dating apps (0.4% >0 min) were judged too rare to analyze.
primary_models.dv: Parent/caregiver-reported CBCL DSM-oriented Affective (depression) Problems scale, 13 items scored 0-2, analyzed as a continuous sum score (scale range 0-26) at Year 5. Analytic sample M = 1.9, SD = 2.9, observed range 0-23 (Table 1). Residuals were right-skewed with many zeros.

primary_models.equation: CBCL_depression[i] = b0 + b1*dating_app_used[i] + b2*dating_app_dont_know[i] + b3*age + b4*sex + b5*race_ethnicity + b6*household_income + b7*parent_education + b8*site + e[i]; reference category = never used; SEs cluster-robust at the family level
primary_models.estimation: Multivariable linear regression reported as standardized beta coefficients, pooled across multiply imputed datasets (MICE with predictive mean matching). Heteroskedasticity-robust (cluster-robust) standard errors clustered at the family level to address heteroskedasticity and non-normality of residuals. Software not reported. No survey weights (baseline weights judged inappropriate for Year 5). Two-sided alpha = 0.05; no multiple-comparison correction. No interaction or stratified analyses. Precision/stability checks and leave-one-site-out analyses reported narratively as stable (no numbers printed). Sensitivity model with additional covariates in Appendix D (see excluded_models). The unadjusted model in Table 2 is reported for comparison.

excluded_models.model: Unadjusted linear regression of CBCL depression on dating app use
excluded_models.why: Transparency comparison; the authors anchor their claim to the adjusted model. Values: used 0.47 (0.12, 0.82), SE 0.18, p = 0.009; don't know -0.02 (-0.39, 0.35), SE 0.19, p = 0.921.

excluded_models.model: Sensitivity model adding daily recreational screen time, cyberbullying victimization, pubertal status, parental screen monitoring, age at first phone owned, average sleep duration, and relationship status
excluded_models.location: Results p. 4; Appendix D (online supplement, not in PDF)
excluded_models.why: Robustness check; authors state results stayed similar and interpret the main adjusted model. Ever used a dating app: beta 0.44 (95% CI 0.03-0.85), p = 0.035. Age at first phone owned is a covariate here, not a focal estimate.
Reported narratively as stable; no numbers printed.

d_transformation.conversion_formula: Coefficients are treated as Y-standardized mean differences for a binary IV (ever used vs never used dating apps), i.e. already on the Cohen's d scale: d = beta. Not passed through r -> d.
d_transformation.contrast_type: Ever used a dating app vs. never used (binary group contrast)
d_transformation.notes: Paper labels them 'standardized betas' without saying which variables were standardized. With a binary IV at 0.9% prevalence a fully standardized beta of 0.42-0.66 is impossible, so they are read as Y-standardized group differences (SD units of the outcome) and used directly as d. Coders should confirm against Appendix E. The paper labels coefficients as standardized betas from linear regression but does not say whether X, Y, or both were standardized. With a binary IV at 0.9% prevalence, a fully standardized beta of 0.42 would be implausibly large, so the value most likely reflects Y-standardized units (i.e., a mean difference of about 0.42 SD of the depression score, d-like) or possibly raw score points. SD_DV for CBCL depression sum score = 2.9 (Table 1, p. 3). SD_IV not reported (binary indicator, 0.9% used, Table 1). Applying r-to-d to 0.42 gives a very different d than passthrough, so the human coder should decide which interpretation applies before conversion. M2 SD_DV not available (Appendix E not in PDF). [complete stage] Verified against full PDF: M1 cluster-robust SEs 0.17 (used) and 0.19 (don't know) added as 'se'; CIs already printed. No supplement file bundled; M2 sd_dv remains unavailable.

extraction_flags: 1) The paper calls its coefficients "standardized beta" but never says which variables were standardized. A fully standardized beta of 0.42 is implausible for a binary IV with 0.9% prevalence, so the value is probably standardized on Y only (d-like) or in raw score points. The r-to-d rule in guidelines 4a gives d of about 0.93, while passing the value through gives d of about 0.42. A human needs to choose before converting. 2) The PDF has only the 6 main-text pages. Appendices A-E are online-only, so the M2 values (youth-reported internalizing, Appendix E: 0.66, 0.34-0.99, p<0.001) and the Appendix D sensitivity values (0.44, 0.03-0.85, p=0.035) come from the Results text and could not be checked against the appendix tables. M2's covariates and N are assumed to match M1. 3) The 'don't know what a dating app is' vs never-used estimate (0.04, -0.33 to 0.41, p=0.817) is included in M1 with a note. It is not a use contrast, so coders may want to strike it. 4) N=11,530 is after multiple imputation of the exposure and the outcome; there are 8,444 complete cases. 5) SD_IV is not reported (binary exposure). SD_DV is 2.9 (Table 1).json
